Article content Then he stood in the courtroom’s prisoner’s box and turned to look at the gallery of about 25 officers, many in uniform, there in support of their colleague, Karl Brown, who was nearly stabbed to death during a wellness check two years ago in a downtown Sarnia condo building. “This corruption runs deep. How dirty are you cops?” a handcuffed Whiteway shouted. The officers didn’t audibly react to Whiteway’s comments, but a couple of soft claps could be heard as Justice Mark Poland found him guilty of both charges he was facing, attempted murder and aggravated assault, and again after the judge dismissed a pair of charter challenges the defence had raised in hopes of having the charges stayed . Whiteway, 37, who was denied bail and has been behind bars for two years, is expected to be sentenced early next year. Article content Ryan Whiteway appears in a Sarnia courtroom by video link from the Sarnia Jail shortly after his arrest in August 2024. Whiteway was convicted Tuesday of attempted murder and aggravated assault in the stabbing of a Sarnia police constable in a downtown condo building on Aug. 20, 2024. (Charles Vincent/Special to Postmedia Network) ‘EMOTIONAL’ REACTION TO VERDICT Brown, after exchanging hugs with several co-workers in the lobby, declined to comment on the outcome. His parents, Fred and Kathy, didn’t want to speak on his behalf, but observed this has weighed heavily on him. “It’s been tough,” Fred Brown said. “It’s a lot of weight off. Emotional,” said a choked-up Reg Musclow, a Sarnia police detective and close friend of Brown’s. Article content Deputy Chief Mike Van Sickle said he was happy for Brown and called the trial part of the healing process. “Although the physical injuries heal, the traumatic effect of an incident like this will last – it could be forever, right? So it’s good that this part is done and the healing can continue,” he said. Detective constables Karl Brown, left, and Erik Ostenfeldt with Sarnia police are shown at the Ontario Medal for Police Bravery ceremony in 2025. Handout ‘HARD FOR HIM TO HEAR’ Whiteway’s lawyer, Nicole DeBellefeuille, said her client maintains what he testified at trial: he thought someone broke into his condo, he didn’t know it was the police, and he wasn’t trying to kill anyone. “It was hard for him to hear that everything he said was rejected,” she said of the judge’s findings. DeBellefeuille said she expected they’d be at the Appeal Court on the issue. She also said she was “particularly shocked” about the findings on their charter challenge and the police’s use of force. THE STABBING AT THE SEAWAY CENTRE On Aug. 20, 2024, Brown, then a 37-year-old Sarnia police constable, was attacked while checking on Whiteway’s well-being inside his 15th-floor Seaway Centre condo. He needed 100 stitches, four blood transfusions and surgery on his thumb. Whiteway, 37, was arrested that night and charged with attempted murder and aggravated assault. Article content At trial, Whiteway testified he thought the officers were aliens there to abduct him. He said he was a paranoid hermit who used drugs such as crystal meth, hash, THC and shatter. When the bathroom door flew open amid the well-being check and a ray of light – Brown’s flashlight – was shone on him, he reached for a self-defence tool, a collector’s knife, and attacked the “entity.” Whiteway was found fit to stand trial after a criminal responsibility assessment , which was ordered in late 2024. While testifying, he also denied wanting to kill Brown and said had he known it was law enforcement, he would have acted differently. He also alleged he was assaulted by three or four Sarnia police officers for five or 10 minutes in what he called a brutal beat-down after his arrest, and again in the back of a cruiser. A Sarnia police cruiser is parked outside the Seaway Centre in Sarnia on Aug. 21, 2024, the day after Sarnia police said one of their officers was stabbed multiple times in the head and neck during a welfare check. (Terry Bridge/Sarnia Observer) CLOSING AND STAY ARGUMENTS DeBellefeuille argued for a stay of the charges due to the alleged police assault. She also argued police had no right to enter her client’s unit and that he acted in self-defence. Prosecutor Nila Mulpuru countered there was no evidence multiple officers assaulted Whiteway and the evidence they did have didn’t support self-defence. She also pointed to exigent circumstances, which allows for searches without warrants to prevent imminent bodily harm. Article content POLAND’S DECISION Poland, who heard the case over five days this summer without a jury, spent more than an hour Tuesday explaining his decisions to convict Whiteway and dismiss the charter challenges. He said this case was about why Whiteway stabbed Brown and what he intended, along with examining the assertion that police had used excessive force. He broke it down into four main issues: ISSUE #1: LAWFUL AUTHORITY TO ENTER Poland found the police did not breach Whiteway’s charter rights by entering his condo without prior authorization. He explained the Crown had to prove on a balance of probabilities their entry was authorized by law and reasonable. In the end, he found their decision to enter Whiteway’s home was justified. He pointed out Whiteway was well-known to police and officers had attended three times by the time Brown and Erik Ostenfeldt, his partner for the well-being check, arrived. They also met with a well-placed source, a neighbour who called police concerned for Whiteway’s well-being after they heard painful, distressed screaming that suddenly stopped, before going to Whiteway’s unit. Poland said the officers waiting about 17 minutes for the master key from a staff member did not diminish the exigent circumstances. And after going inside, he found they did what was expected of them by going into the locked bathroom amid their concerns for his well-being. Advertisement 6 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content The judge also said police conduct must be assessed in the circumstances as they appeared at the time, not in hindsight. ISSUE #2: SELF-DEFENCE Poland said it was up to the Crown to neutralize the defence’s self-defence argument – and it did. He pointed to part of the law that says the act committed must be reasonable in the circumstances. Poland said it wasn’t reasonable for Whiteway to stab Brown if he knew Brown was a police officer. The judge found Whiteway did know this, despite his repeated denials. Police had been at his door 22 times in the past, according to Whiteway’s own testimony, and he also recorded a video through the peephole that night, which shows Brown and Ostenfeldt wearing their uniforms. Whiteway can be heard saying, “Yeah, head out, boy,” after the staffer gives them the master key and, “It’s going to get rough in here, boy,” shortly before they enter. Poland said he found Whiteway was aware police were there and intended to enter and the video demonstrated he didn’t adopt a panic room mode in response to unknown attendants, as he had testified. An email Whiteway sent shortly before the clash also was important in ascertaining his state of knowledge as it included the phrase “unauthorized entry,” which points to his knowing it was police, Poland said. Article content A Sarnia police cruiser is parked outside the Seaway Centre in Sarnia on Aug. 21, 2024, the day after Sarnia police said one of their officers was stabbed multiple times in the head and neck during a welfare check. Terry Bridge/Sarnia Observer/Postmedia Network Photo by Terry Bridge / Terry Bridge/The Observer ISSUE #3: INTENT TO MURDER The Crown also had to prove the specific intent to murder beyond a reasonable doubt, Poland explained. Once again, it did. The judge rejected Whiteway’s testimony that he just attacked at the light. He pointed out the majority of the blows were inflicted on the vital and exposed parts of Brown’s body, such as his head and neck. He also used army-style knives and the element of surprise and stabbed from a position of tactical advantage. After reviewing all the evidence, Poland said he was left without reasonable doubt Whiteway intended to murder Brown and convicted him. “I’m not going back to school for police foundations,” Whiteway uttered from the prisoner’s box in response. ISSUE #4: CRUEL AND UNUSUAL PUNISHMENT As for the cruel and unusual punishment charter argument, Poland said after rejecting Whiteway’s testimony he was left with no evidence that happened. Photos of damaged drywall with blood stains in his unit were not sufficient on their own. Poland noted Ostenfeldt had Brown’s blood mainly on the back of his uniform and there could have been incidental blood transfer on the wall. All of the officers denied assaulting Whiteway and the judge rejected Whiteway’s assertion he was beaten by three to four officers over five to 10 minutes. Advertisement 8 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content Sgt. Josh Mitchell testified a handcuffed Whiteway resisted arrest while he was briefly in a one-in-one situation with him and he had to turn custody over to other officers, worrying he would lose control after seeing his close friend, Brown, hurt and possibly dying. But Mitchell said he did not recall punching Whiteway or damaging the drywall. Poland noted Whiteway did not link any of the damage to the one-on-one encounter with Mitchell, just to an alleged group beat-down, which the judge said clearly did not occur. The judge did say he found it unusual Mitchell was the only officer who said Whiteway resisted and that he directed the other officers out of the unit and was left alone with him. He added he had significant concerns about Mitchell’s reliability and credibility, raising questions about the precise nature of the application of force that did occur. But, with Whiteway’s credibility and reliability sorely imperiled, he was left with no evidence that Whiteway was assaulted. Whiteway also failed to point out any physical characteristics of the officer who allegedly punched him in the back of the cruiser, despite being in close proximity, the judge said. ‘WELL-ARTICULATED’ JUDGEMENT Van Sickle called Poland’s decision a well-articulated, well-researched and methodical evaluation of the evidence. “So I was very appreciative of that,” the deputy chief said. As for the assault allegations against their officers, Musclow said DeBellefeuille is a tenacious, very good defence lawyer who went over everything with a fine-tooth comb. “As you saw in the verdict from the judge, they were unfounded,” Musclow added. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Construction in the Jewish settlement of Alfei Menashe on the West Bank Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Construction in the Jewish settlement of Alfei Menashe on the West Bank Photograph: Amir Levy/Getty Images Foreign policy Senior UK rabbis come out in support of sanctions on Israeli settlements Spiritual leaders stress diversity of views within Jewish community and warn against inaction on settler violence ‘It’s a good start’: prominent Israelis welcome UK sanctions Aamna Mohdin Community affairs correspondent Wed 9 Sep 2026 13.57 EDT Last modified on Wed 9 Sep 2026 15.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Prominent British rabbis have backed Ed Miliband’s sanctions on Israeli settlements, warning that the time for inaction on settler violence must come to an end. The intervention comes after the UK’s chief rabbi, the spiritual leader of mainstream Orthodox Jews in the UK, Sir Ephraim Mirvis, described UK sanctions against illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories as a “dark day for British Jews” and warned they could embolden people who “use hatred as a weapon against Jews”. The sanctions were also condemned by the Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership council. Miliband rejects chief rabbi’s claim that West Bank sanctions put UK Jews at risk Read more But other senior rabbis, many from the progressive wing of the community, have come forward to stress the diversity of views within the British Jewish community, with some backing Miliband’s sanctions , while others warned that concern about the measures should not become an excuse for ignoring settler violence and expansion, and others calling for the government to go further. Jonathan Wittenberg, a senior rabbi of Masorti Judaism , said he was in the Palestinian village of Umm al Khair while Miliband was delivering his speech, and had seen the results of settler violence “with my own eyes”. “What is taking place today in the West Bank is a Chillul HaShem, a violation of God’s name of the worst order. We cannot stay silent. This is terrible for Palestinian people who want to get on with their lives in peace. It is terrible for Israel,” he said. Wittenberg added: “We must speak out. We must do so out of deep concern for what is human and just, and for the sake of Israel and Judaism. We cannot turn away.” While he acknowledged that the British Jewish community did not have to agree with everything the British government chose to do, he said: “The time is for action.” Rabbi Alexandra Wright from the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in London, vice-chair of the British Friends of Rabbis for Human Rights, said while not everyone in the community would support the sanctions, action was needed as “the occupation and escalating violence are harming Palestinians and Israelis”. ‘It’s a good start’: prominent Israelis welcome UK sanctions on illegal settlements Read more She said: “The sanctions are the UK’s commitment to a two-state solution. The Anglo-Jewish community is committed to a Jewish state that is founded, not on oppression and violence, but, in the words of Israel’s declaration of independence, ‘on freedom, justice and peace as envisaged by the prophets of Israel’.” Wright, who had recently visited the Palestinian village Umm al-Khair, which has faced relentless attacks by Israeli settlers, called on the Jewish community to “not hold back any progression towards a two-state solution”. Jeremy Gordon, the rabbi of New London Synagogue, who came out in favour of Miliband’s sanctions, said: “It is wrong to argue for silence, inaction or ‘the use of carrots’ – appeasement – before the settler movement and those who support it. The playbook of these settlers is predicated on the notion that they will be appeased or ignored, and that well-meaning Jews the world over overlook their illegal and criminal actions.” Lev Taylor, rabbi of Kingston Liberal Synagogue in London, described the sanctions as a sign “the government is moving in the right direction”. He added: “Some of my Israeli members have been campaigning for sanctions exactly like this … The Judaism in which I believe repudiates this brutal occupation.” He pointed to the statements from the Israeli member of the Knesset Gilad Kariv, who said: “The blame for the European countries’ announcement of sanctions falls squarely on the shoulders of [Benjamin] Netanyahu, [Bezalel] Smotrich, [Israel] Katz , and [Gideon] Sa’ar.” There is some consternation within the Orthodox community at the suggestion British Jews are uniformly opposed to the sanctions. Miliband, the foreign secretary, announced the sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, with the government taking the position that Israel’s occupation of the Palestinian territory was unlawful. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The measures were coordinated with France, Canada and nine other countries that were also introducing sanctions on Israel over the increasing expansion of settlements, which the UK government says is threatening the future of a Palestinian state. Jonathan Boyd, the executive director for Institute for Jewish Policy Research, explained there are no robust survey data on whether British Jews support sanctions on Israeli settlements specifically. “However, the available evidence shows that views on Israeli government policy and the conflict are quite diverse, varying by age, denomination and political outlook. “At the same time, they also show that most British Jews feel a strong emotional attachment to Israel and have become increasingly concerned about antisemitism in Britain since October 7.” Rabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy, co-leaders of Progressive Judaism, which represents about one-third of Jews affiliated to synagogues and estimates the same proportion of non-affiliated Jews share its values, described sanctions as a “clumsy tool” that could have unintended consequences. But they said that “measures directed at Israeli settlements are not the same as an attack on Jews. We should take care not to collapse the distinction between them.” View image in fullscreen Rabbi Charley Baginsky and Rabbi Josh Levy. Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian They called on those against sanctions to offer more than statements condemning violence, adding: “Inaction is not neutral. It too is a political and moral choice.” Wittenberg, Baginsky and Levy all asserted their opposition to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement , and welcomed Miliband’s stance against it. Tuesday’s sanctions announcement prompted a swift backlash from Israel, which ordered the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem and banned 12 British MPs and activists from entering Israel. Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, threatened that the US could take retaliatory action over trade, but the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US would “obviously” not follow the UK government’s actions but did not want to see the West Bank destabilised. The UK foreign secretary said he regretted what the Israeli government had announced but was “proud of what we did yesterday and it was the right thing to do”. Miliband accepted the closure of the British consulate in Jerusalem would be “damaging” but said the government had “weighed up the costs and benefits in advance of this”. The Eastern Flank: Coordination of Allied forces put to the test At Cincu (central Romania) and other locations across the country, Romanian and Allied troops have recently taken part in the "Carpathian Arc 2026" exercise. Photo: Headquarters Multinational Division South-East Agenția Media a Armatei , 28.10.2026, 14:00 At Cincu (central Romania) and other locations across the country, Romanian and Allied troops have recently taken part in the “Carpathian Arc 2026” exercise. Within a simulated combat scenario, they analyzed intelligence regarding the adversary, planned operations, and coordinated the actions of the participating units. The exercise was led by the Headquarters Multinational Corps South-East in Sibiu (central Romania) and included an evaluation for the recertification of the Headquarters Multinational Division South-East in Bucharest. French Brigadier General Cyril Mathias, the Deputy Division Commander, spoke about the importance of field-testing the procedures and equipment: “Operational readiness must be sustained through training. We cannot improve our level of preparedness without training regularly and testing our procedures, techniques, and equipment in the field. This was the primary conclusion, and, perhaps, the most important one.” The procedures were implemented by teams composed of military personnel from several countries. Within the division’s operations center, differences in language and experience necessitated a clear and concise mode of communication. French Major Baudot, who led this center during the exercise, explained: “Because we spoke different languages ​​and had different customs, we needed simple procedures. We had to be able to deliver short, precise briefings. That is what we did within the Alliance: we found a way to work as efficiently as possible.” For Captain Pablo Carpena of the Spanish Army, the exercise also marked his first experience in such a role within the current operations structure. He worked in a team consisting primarily of Romanian military personnel and appreciated how well he was integrated: “The team was composed mainly of Romanians, nearly 85%. Consequently, I spent most of my time working alongside them. They were very open to welcoming military personnel from other countries into the team. From my perspective, the collaboration was excellent and yielded very good results.” The scenario also incorporated lessons drawn from the war in Ukraine. Military personnel examined how to adapt the command’s operational approach to the use of drones on the battlefield. The head of the division’s intelligence branch explained the rationale behind introducing these scenarios into the exercise: “Preparations for this exercise began early in the year. What I want to emphasize is that we are taking lessons identified in Ukraine, such as the use of drones, and attempting to integrate them into this exercise. Why? To determine the most effective way for us to respond.” The experience of the war in Ukraine also served as a benchmark for adapting Allied procedures. Brigadier General Cyril Mathias highlighted that the exercise provided a framework for incorporating these lessons into the division’s training: “This exercise offered a unique opportunity to put into practice all the lessons identified from the ongoing conflict and to integrate into our procedures the innovations necessary to account for these lessons. And the conflict in Ukraine was, of course, our main point of reference.” The multinational exercise “Carpathian Arc 2026” concluded with the recertification of the Headquarters Multinational Division Southeast in Bucharest. For Romanian and Allied military, it served as a test of their ability to jointly plan and conduct operations for the defense of the North Atlantic Alliance’s eastern flank. (Alexandra Rădescu, tr.
